title: The Personalization Arms Race: When Scammers Know Your Customers Too
summary: The Personalization Arms Race is changing fraud prevention. See how AI helps scammers personalize attacks and how you can fight back.
body_markdown:
For years, the badly written phishing email had one useful quality: it often looked exactly like a badly written phishing email. The greeting was generic, the language slightly (occasionally extremely) off, and the proposition had very little to do with the person receiving it. Even when scams were effective, there was often a visible gap between a genuinely personal interaction and a mass-produced one.


That gap is getting much harder to see. ‘Dear valued customer’ messages are disappearing. A scammer can now approach you knowing where you work, referencing the conference you attended last week, or the subjects you talk about online. None of that necessarily requires a sophisticated hack. The raw material is all there, sitting across social media, professional profiles, public records, online forums, and previous data breaches.


Businesses have spent years trying to understand customers well enough to make their communications more relevant. The uncomfortable reality is that scammers are discovering the value of personalization too. In this article, we’ll look at the personalization arms race that scammers are in with financial organizations and their customers.


## Turning A Digital Footprint Into A Digital Dossier


It’s tempting to think of a digital footprint as simply the things we choose to share online, but in reality, it’s much broader than that.


Assembling the picture doesn’t have to be a painstaking manual exercise anymore. AI can help gather, sort, and connect information from multiple sources, turning a scattered digital footprint into something closer to a usable briefing document. Taken together, this collection of ordinary details can make an approach feel credible.


This is bigger than a warning to ‘share less online’ too. Much of this information is not something any of us can realistically keep private, after all. Our jobs may require public biographies and LinkedIn profiles. Businesses publish details about employees and events. Our friends and family share information about us, and vast data breaches happen regularly.


The real change is that all this information can now be gathered and repurposed much more efficiently by the very last people you’d want doing that job.


## How AI Turns Research Into Reconnaissance At Scale


Businesses have spent years getting better at personalization: we all know that relevance works. The uncomfortable truth is that exactly the same principle applies to scammers.


Social media makes that especially visible. According to the US Federal Trade Commission (FTC), nearly 30% of people who reported losing money to a scam last year[said it had started on social media, with reported losses reaching $2.1 billion](https://search.ftc.gov/news-events/news/press-releases/2026/04/new-ftc-data-show-people-have-lost-billions-social-media-scams) .


An Instagram ad can be aimed at someone interested in a particular type of investment. Once they click, the interaction changes. The scammer has a lead, a little more information, and an opportunity to begin tailoring the conversation around that individual.


That pattern is already visible at scale.[The FTC says nearly 60% of people](https://www.ftc.gov/news-events/news/press-releases/2026/04/new-ftc-data-show-people-have-lost-billions-social-media-scams) who reported losing money to a romance scam in 2025 said it began on social media. Scammers researching their victims is nothing new – a determined criminal has always been able to look someone up, learn about their interests, and use that information to craft an approach. What’s changing is the amount of work required to do it, and therefore the number of people who can be targeted in this way.


Publicly available information, leaked data, and social activity can be combined by AI into hyper-personalized scams at scale, using highly customized messages and conversations. The result no longer has to be reserved for a small number of carefully researched, high-value targets. The same operation can potentially research far more people, identify what might resonate with each of them, and tailor the approach accordingly. What used to resemble manual detective work starts to become automated mass reconnaissance.


## What Can Organizations Actually Do About It?


Organizations need to assume an attacker may already know quite a lot about the customer. On their own, an address, employer, recent travel, interests, or even aspects of their financial life is no longer useful evidence that someone is who they claim to be.


That changes the job we ask personal data to do. Instead of relying on knowledge as proof of identity, organizations need to build confidence from a wider combination of signals and pay much closer attention to context.


### 1. Stop using personal knowledge as proof


For years, authentication has often depended on information assumed to be difficult for anyone else to know (like an address or date of birth). The trouble is that many of those facts are now discoverable or purchasable.


So, while a caller who knows a customer’s details may sound convincing, that knowledge should increasingly be treated as context rather than proof. Authentication needs to lean more heavily on things an attacker can’t simply research, such as possession of a trusted device, secure in-app confirmation, or other independently verified credentials.


### 2. Look at what the customer is doing (not just what they know)


As personal information becomes easier to acquire, behavior becomes more valuable. Someone may have passed the identity checks and still be doing something highly unusual.


Does the customer normally use this device? Is this payment destination new? Is the value unusually high? Has the customer suddenly changed the way they move through an account or interact with the organization? Is the request consistent with what they normally do?


None of those signals necessarily prove that a scam is taking place. But, taken together, they can reveal something a well-researched attacker may struggle to reproduce: the customer’s normal pattern of behavior.


### 3. Personalize the protection as well as the experience


If scammers are getting better at tailoring their approaches, organizations can get better at tailoring their prevention. Generic fraud warnings are easy to tune out. A warning becomes far more useful when it relates to what the customer is actually doing.


Someone making their first transfer to a cryptocurrency platform may need a different intervention from someone paying a new tradesperson, responding to an investment opportunity, or sending money to someone they met online.


Rather than bombard customers with warnings, the aim is to use customer context to make the right intervention more relevant and timely. In other words, organizations can apply some of the same principles that have made personalization valuable in marketing and customer experience to scam prevention as well.


The scammer uses context to make the deception more persuasive, but organizations can use context to make the protection more effective.


### 4. Treat customer data as part of the fraud attack surface


Privacy teams understandably ask whether data is sensitive, whether it’s needed, and who should have access to it. Fraud teams may need to add another question: how useful would this information be to somebody trying to manipulate the customer?


A data point that appears relatively harmless on its own can become much more powerful when combined with others. Employer, age, travel history, buying behavior, and contact details might collectively give an attacker enough material to construct a highly credible story.


Privacy, cybersecurity, and fraud prevention have to work much more closely together. Data minimization and access controls shouldn’t be seen simply as compliance measures. Protecting customer information also removes ingredients that might otherwise be used to make future scams more convincing.


### 5. Design for an attacker who has done their homework


Here’s the biggest shift in mindset: we need to stop designing fraud controls around the (almost always) erroneous assumption that the scammer knows less than the organization does.


In reality, they may know the customer’s name, job, interests, and recent activity. They may understand the language the organization uses and be able to imitate its communications. They may even know enough about the customer’s circumstances to make an approach feel uncannily well timed.


So, instead of keeping every personal fact secret, good defense has to depend on controls that remain effective, even when some of those facts might already be compromised.


That means stronger authentication, richer behavioral context, better-timed customer interventions, and a more integrated view of the data that could help an attacker build trust. The goal should be to make sure that a scammer simply knowing a lot about a potential victim is no longer enough to pass as someone they trust.


## Conclusion: Knowing Your Customer Works Both Ways


Businesses have spent decades getting better at knowing their customers. That has brought obvious benefits: more relevant communications, better service, and targeted experiences. But the same abundance of data that makes personalization possible also changes the economics of deception. Scammers can use many of the same signals to decide whom to target, what might interest them, and how best to make an approach feel credible.


That doesn’t mean organizations should abandon personalization, or that customers should somehow disappear from the internet. It does mean we need to be more realistic about what personal knowledge proves. We need to design authentication that does not depend on facts that can be researched, use behavioral and contextual signals more intelligently, make scam warnings more relevant, and treat customer data as part of the fraud attack surface rather than simply a privacy concern.


[Because in the personalization arms race, the challenge is making sure that knowing your customer is not enough for a scammer to become someone they trust.](https://www.concentrix.com/services-solutions/financial-crimes-compliance/)
